questions.q: What does a triggered pipeline do?
options: Processes everything currently available across every table, in dependency order, then shuts down
Runs indefinitely, never stopping
Only processes one table at a time, never the full dependency graph
Requires manual intervention to determine when to stop
questions.explain: This is Lesson 33's trigger(availableNow=True) concept, applied at the whole-pipeline level.

questions.q: How does continuous mode differ from triggered mode?
options: It starts up and keeps running indefinitely, processing new data as it arrives, with no next scheduled run to wait for
It processes data less frequently than triggered mode
It cannot be used with @dlt.expect rules
It only works with @dlt.view, never @dlt.table
questions.explain: This is Lesson 33's trigger(processingTime=...) concept, at the whole-pipeline level.

questions.q: What's the real cost difference between triggered and continuous compute lifecycles?
options: Triggered is billed only while actually running (spins up, processes, spins down); continuous is billed continuously since the cluster stays up indefinitely
Both cost exactly the same regardless of usage pattern
Continuous mode is always cheaper because it avoids startup overhead
Triggered mode requires a permanently running cluster too
questions.explain: This echoes the same cost tradeoff Lesson 5 (job vs. all-purpose clusters) and Lesson 23 (maintenance isn't constant) touched on.

questions.q: Why would triggered mode be the right choice for this course's monthly NYC Taxi data?
options: The data arrives in monthly files — genuinely infrequent, bursty ingestion — so paying for continuously-running compute between files would be wasteful
Triggered mode is always the only valid choice for any data source
NYC Taxi data arrives every second, requiring continuous mode
Triggered mode cannot process CSV files
questions.explain: Continuous mode earns its cost for sources generating events by the second, like real-time sensor data.

questions.q: What determines whether triggered or continuous mode is the right choice for a given pipeline?
options: Matching the mode to the source's real ingestion cadence, not choosing one by default
Always choosing continuous mode for maximum freshness regardless of cost
Always choosing triggered mode regardless of how frequently data arrives
The choice has no real cost or performance implications either way
questions.explain: A source generating events by the second is where continuous mode's cost is actually justified.
